question: Which statement best describes Render phase vs commit phase?
options: Keys give sibling elements a stable identity so reconciliation can match an element to its previous instance across reorders rather than matching by position. They only need to be unique among siblings and should be derived from data identity, never the array index for lists that can reorder, insert, or delete. The classic gotcha: index keys make React reuse the DOM node (and its uncontrolled state) at a position while only swapping text, so checkbox/input state desyncs from the data after a sort.

React splits an update into two phases: the render phase calls your components to compute the new element tree and reconciles it against the previous one — it is pure, side-effect-free, and (under concurrency) interruptible — while the commit phase applies the resulting DOM mutations and runs effects, and is synchronous and atomic. This split is why side effects must live in effects, not the component body: the render phase can run multiple times or be discarded, but commit happens exactly once per update. useLayoutEffect runs during commit before paint; useEffect runs after paint.

Reconciliation is the algorithm that compares the new element tree with the previously committed one to determine the minimal DOM changes. It runs on heuristics: elements of different types are torn down and rebuilt (discarding state), same-type elements are updated in place, and lists are matched by key. Understanding it explains remount-vs-update behavior — for instance, changing an element's type or key forces a full unmount and remount.

The Virtual DOM is an in-memory tree of plain JavaScript objects (React elements) describing what the UI should look like, living entirely in JS memory where the browser never sees it. It exists so React can compute a minimal set of real DOM operations by diffing two descriptions instead of mutating the DOM ad hoc. A key nuance for interviews: the Virtual DOM is not inherently faster than the DOM — it trades JS diffing work for fewer, batched, well-targeted DOM mutations.

A component re-renders when its own state changes, its props change, its parent re-renders, or a context it consumes changes. Crucially, a parent re-render re-runs ALL descendants by default, regardless of whether their props changed — which is why memoization exists. The key insight is that re-running a component function is not the same as changing the DOM: React still commits only what actually differs, so many 're-renders' are invisible to the user.

Batching is React grouping multiple state updates into a single render to avoid intermediate renders. Since React 18, automatic batching applies everywhere — event handlers, promises, setTimeout, native event callbacks — not just React event handlers as before. This means several setState calls in one tick produce one render and one commit, improving performance; flushSync can opt out when you genuinely need a synchronous DOM update between two updates.

The Fiber tree is React's internal linked data structure where each node (a fiber) represents a component instance or DOM element and a unit of work. It replaced the old synchronous recursive reconciler so React can process work incrementally, pause, resume, and prioritize it — the foundation for concurrent rendering. During an update React builds a work-in-progress fiber tree, diffs it, and on commit swaps it to become the current tree.
